comparison: Both evaluate neurophysiological evidence (C54-C65, C87) regarding branch-specific effects. OpenEval finds the evidence clearly supports hierarchical processing and refutes flat models. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, noting that both research groups agree on the finding but disagree on interpretation—H&M argues the data is 'most compatible with the flat model' while authors argue it refutes flat models.

Both address temporal ordering in V1 activity and serial processing claims (C93-C97, C144-C146). OpenEval finds the temporal evidence clearly supports serial processing and refutes flat models. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, questioning the relevance of mental curve tracing tasks to hierarchical decision-making and whether this evidence generalizes to simpler tasks.

Both evaluate evidence about parallel-to-serial shifts with task complexity (C102-C108, C122-C123). OpenEval finds this well-supported by psychophysical kernel evidence. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, questioning whether evidence from complex tasks (two branching points) necessarily implies hierarchical processing in simpler tasks, suggesting strategy may shift with complexity.

Both address the overarching flexibility conclusion (C115-C120). OpenEval finds the flexibility claim well-supported by diverse experimental evidence showing both parallel and serial processing. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, noting that the conclusion depends on accepting individual results that remain contested throughout their review.

Both evaluate claims about alternative mechanisms and modulatory signals (C68-C74). OpenEval finds the discussion of alternative mechanisms reasonable and well-supported by literature. Peer reviewers rate this SUPPORTED, explicitly requesting this discussion and finding the authors' response about expected hierarchical mechanisms adequate.

Both address neurophysiological constraints on the H&M model (C38-C41, C84-C85). OpenEval finds the critique of exponential firing rate increases and biological implausibility well-supported. Peer reviewers rate this SUPPORTED, not challenging the neurophysiological critique, though they focused more on behavioral predictions.

Both evaluate behavioral evidence from model simulations and RT data (C48-C52, C86, C142-C143). OpenEval finds clear quantitative mismatch supporting the claims. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, noting the task lacked reaction time design and that H&M's revised model with collapsing bounds addresses the RT issue, suggesting the original rejection may have been premature.

OpenEval R8 addresses H&M model variants and simulation results (C46-C47, C142-C143), finding clear evidence of model limitations. This overlaps with peer R1's concerns about RT data and model adequacy, where reviewers note that additional mechanisms like collapsing bounds might resolve the issues.

OpenEval R4 addresses H&M model failures (C86-C88). Peer R1 shares concern about C86, rating the overall behavioral evidence UNCERTAIN due to task design issues and the possibility that revised models could address the concerns.

OpenEval R9 critiques model assumptions including self-excitation consequences (C81-C85). Peer R5 addresses overlapping neurophysiological concerns (C84-C85) and rates them SUPPORTED, accepting the biological realism critique.

OpenEval found that H&M model features including self-excitation and high bounds relate to flat kernels (C35-C37), with supporting citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific model characterization claims.

OpenEval evaluated discussion of attractor networks as potential solution (C42-C43), finding it appropriate speculation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these theoretical alternative mechanism claims.

OpenEval evaluated critique of H&M's parsimony claims (C77-C80), finding it appropriate given demonstrated model failures. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these parsimony argument claims.

OpenEval evaluated claims about task structure differences between studies (C98-C101), finding them reasonable inferences from experimental designs. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though related to peer concerns about task complexity in R4.

OpenEval evaluated methodological claims about data collection and analysis procedures (C128-C133), finding them clearly stated and appropriate. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these methodological description claims.
